forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Hart forecasts £434k more investment income than budgeted and £627k above budget on fees
news_drafts.lead:
Hart District Council expects to earn £1.2m from investing its cash this year, £434k more than the £766k it budgeted, according to its second-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget) for 2026/27, reported to its Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 13 October. Total income from fees and charges is forecast at £7.57m against a budget of £6.94m, a gain of £627k.

The budget assumed interest rates would fall; they have stayed higher. The paper says "political uncertainty has delayed the reduction in forecast interest rate reductions." Its treasury model draws on forecasts from the council's financial advisers, Link Group, and the paper cautions that "fluctuations in interest rates together with cash flow changes can change this number." Interest payable is as budgeted.

Several services account for the fee gain. Planning development fees are forecast at £975k against £841k, a gain of £134k. Waste income, including green waste subscriptions and recycling materials, is £2.11m against £2.0m, up £112k. Building control is £325k against £270k, up £55k, and off-street parking £1.07m against £1.02m, up £48k.

On capital spending (money spent on things that last), two housing schemes are forecast to spend well below budget. Rural exception site funding is forecast at £88k against £350k, and top-up funding for rented affordable housing at £79k against £315k. Both are multi-year projects.

news_drafts.headline: Hart's auditors expect a qualified opinion on 2025/26 accounts and an unqualified one by 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Hart District Council's external auditors expect to give a qualified opinion on its 2025/26 accounts, meaning they will not be able to fully sign off the accounts. They anticipate that a clean, unqualified opinion "may be achievable by 2027/28", according to a draft audit results report put to the council's Audit Committee on 6 October.

The council is taking part in the government's audit recovery programme, run by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. It follows disclaimer opinions on the accounts for 2022/23 and 2023/24, in which the auditors said they could not form a view on the accounts at all. A qualified opinion for 2025/26 would be a step up from that position.

The auditors say limits on their assurance remain over the council's reserves, the money it has put aside, which are affected by the problems in earlier years' accounts. They also cite the consequences of past valuations of property, plant and equipment, the land, buildings and other physical assets the council owns. The report says the 2027/28 forecast is subject to "the successful completion of all planned audit procedures".

findings.headline: Energy efficiency projects at leisure centres showing significant delays
findings.detail: Frogmore LC solar, BEMS and insulation project is forecast at £10k against a £134k budget (variance £124k). The Frogmore LC heat pumps project shows variance of £132k against a £1,445k budget. The solar/BEMS project is noted as savings from procurement process.
findings.matters: Energy efficiency and decarbonisation are strategic priorities for councils facing budget pressures. Slippage on these schemes affects progress toward environmental targets and may indicate cost overruns or procurement delays that would carry into 2027-28 and beyond.
findings.figures: Solar/BEMS: budget £134k, forecast £10k, variance (£124k); Heat pumps: budget £1,445k, forecast £1,314k, variance (£132k)

findings.headline: Rural housing and affordable housing top-up funding significantly underspent
findings.detail: Rural Exception Site Funding is forecast at £88k against a £350k budget (variance £263k) and Top-up Rented Affordable Housing is forecast at £79k against a £315k budget (variance £236k). Both are noted as multi-year projects, indicating these represent timing shifts rather than scheme cancellations.
findings.matters: Underspend on housing development funding may indicate challenges in securing sites, partners or consents for affordable housing delivery, an area of council strategic focus and external scrutiny from the housing crisis.
findings.figures: Rural Exception: budget £350k, forecast £88k, variance (£263k); Top-up: budget £315k, forecast £79k, variance (£236k)

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation 4x1bed project forecast to overspend by £200k
findings.detail: While most capital projects are underspending, the 4x1bed temporary accommodation scheme shows forecast spend of £1,000k against a revised budget of £800k, a variance of £200k over budget. This is the only significant overspend across the entire capital programme.
findings.matters: Cost pressures on temporary housing are a key concern for finance directors and audit focus given welfare pressures. An emerging overspend here is noteworthy against a backdrop of general underspends elsewhere and signals rising costs in this service area.

findings.headline: Heathlands Remodelling project spending forecast at 33% of £2m budget
findings.detail: Heathlands Remodelling shows a variance of £1.35m against a £2m revised budget, with forecast spending of only £650k. The project is noted as multi-year with £875k planned for 2027-28, indicating the delivery schedule has extended from the current financial year.
findings.matters: This is the single largest variance in the programme. Housing delivery is a strategic priority and audit focus; significant slippage on a major capital project may indicate delivery capacity constraints or scope changes.

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast £2.3m under revised budget at Q2 2026-27
findings.detail: The revised capital budget of £15.7m is forecast to deliver £13.4m of spend, a variance of £2.3m or 14.8% under budget. This comprises £2.0m underspend in Community capital projects and £312k underspend in Corporate capital projects, with the shortfall reflecting several deferred or delayed schemes noted as multi-year projects.
findings.matters: Significant variance in capital spending affects treasury management, borrowing requirements, and service delivery planning. A lender needs to understand whether slippages are timing shifts or permanent deferrals, and whether forecast reliability is being maintained.
